web_evidence.title: Dear John official PDF excerpt
web_evidence.note: The author-hosted 26-page excerpt contains the prologue and opening of Part I. John narrates both, identifies himself as John Tyree, and consistently recounts his own life as “I.”

web_evidence.title: A Study on Father and Son Relationship in Nicholas Sparks’ Dear John
web_evidence.note: This scholarly close-reading article explicitly states that the novel is written in first-person point of view and analyzes John Tyree across all three parts.

search_log: Searched “Nicholas Sparks Dear John official excerpt first chapter narrator John” and “site:nicholassparks.com Dear John excerpt”; opened the author-hosted 26-page PDF covering the prologue and opening chapters.
Searched “Dear John Nicholas Sparks point of view first person narrator”; opened the 2012 RAINBOW/Lexicon scholarly article explicitly describing the novel’s first-person point of view.

Searched for publisher, ReadingGroupGuides, Bookreporter, and Google Books excerpts. ReadingGroupGuides and Bookreporter results indicated permission-based excerpts, but their pages failed to open reliably, so they were not used as evidence.

Ran targeted exact-quote searches for the mirror passage, the breakup letter, the full-moon passage, “Everything around me makes me miss you,” and the final time passage. These identified Savannah’s embedded letter and several film-script or letter-voice-over lines, preventing their local first person from being treated as base narration.

Searched for alternating POV, multiple narrators, epistolary structure, and Savannah narration; found no credible evidence that the novel sustains a second base narrator or changes grammatical person.
person_note: The controlling narrator is John Tyree, who participates in the story and narrates his life in first person. Numerous event quotes independently expose this voice, including explicit framing of “our story,” while the authorized opening identifies the narrator by name and sustains the same perspective. The scholarly whole-book analysis corroborates that all three parts use first-person point of view. Apparent contrary first-person material from Savannah belongs to embedded letters or dialogue, and several dataset quotations derive from the film’s correspondence voice-overs; none establishes an autonomous base section. The main residual uncertainty concerns the provenance and clipping of a few individual Goodreads quotations, not the novel-level classification.
